## Paper

## Abstract

Volcanic risk escalates significantly during unrest. In late 2021, the Italian island of Vulcano entered into a phase of unrest featuring Very Long Period seismic events, which are considered to be markers of magma and gas flowing across the volcanic plumbing system. Here we show how Neural Network Nodal Ambient Noise Tomography generates a high-resolution shear-wave velocity model for investigating the causative drivers of Vulcano’s unrest. Using a deep learning model we harvest seismic dispersion data from a dense nodal seismic network deployed during the early unrest’s phase. The inverted 3-D model reveals a high-resolution tomography of the shallow part of a volcanic system in unrest. If deployed and rapidly processed in (near) real-time during periods of unrest, Neural Network Nodal Ambient Noise Tomography can lead to dynamic and adaptive evacuation plans. Such advances would contribute to more effective, source-dependent risk mitigation schemes in volcanic regions, potentially saving lives.

---

## Introduction

The island of Vulcano, along with Lipari and Salina, constitutes the central volcanic ridge of the Aeolian archipelago on the Tyrrhenian Sea, southern Italy (Fig. 1A). This central sector is aligned with the NNW-SSE regional Aeolian-Tindari-Letojanni (ATLF) strike-slip fault system1–4 (Fig. 1A–B). Vulcano experienced multiple Vulcanian-style eruptions with frequent transitions from magmatic to phreatomagmatic activity5, and has remained quiescent since its last eruption in 1888-1890 AD. However, below La Fossa caldera (Fig. 1C), the primary volcanic feature of Vulcano, an active hydrothermal system at a depth of between 0.5 and 1 km below sea level (b.s.l.)6–8 has been intermittently affected by episodic inputs of magmatic fluids and volcanic degassing unrest over the past four decades9,10. Considering the importance of the island for tourists, the exposure to volcanic hazards remains exceedingly high even for minor eruptive events or episodes of increased degassing3,11,12.

Since early September 2021, La Fossa caldera exhibited increased activity characterized by a rapid intensification of previously unseen unrest indicators8,12–16. This activity was marked by a large rate of increase in fumarolic temperatures, accompanied by substantial emissions of CO2-rich and SO2 magmatic gases and diffuse soil fluxes8,10,13,14,16. A centimeter-scale uplift was also observed at La Fossa, along with a significant increase of local seismicity, and the detection of Very Long Period (VLP) seismic signals8,14–16. VLPs are a distinctive feature of this unrest as they are usually attributed to the release of magma and/or pressurized magmatic fluids through the shallow fractured volcanic conduits12,14,16–18. Although the unrest phase is no longer at its peak, and the yellow alert level declared by the Italian Civil Protection on October 1st 2021 was set back to green on December 19th 202319, an increase in VLP events, fumaroles temperatures and gas emissions was detected again starting from May 202420. The current unrest shares similarities with Vulcano’s previous crisis of the late 1970s to early 1990s16, suggesting that the current episode may continue for several more years21.

The latest conceptual models discussing this unrest suggest either the persistent degassing, at a reduced rate, of a deep-seated magmatic source at about 4-5 km depth8, or increased activity of the shallow hydrothermal system16,21. In the past, some authors proposed the replenishment of the shallow hydrothermal system with magmatic fluids originating from the pulsating degassing process of a deeper, pressurized, and stationary magmatic body5,7–9,11–14,22,23. Nonetheless, Vulcano’s plumbing system is believed to be a polybaric intricate magmatic network with reservoirs having sill and dike-like structures8,11,22. Unfortunately, the geophysical data are sparse and mainly constrained by airborne geophysics24–27. Onshore studies do not penetrate enough in the plumbing system to reveal the interplay between magmatic and hydrothermal fluids28–30. Only recent investigations have shown the plumbing system down to a few kilometers depth but none of them had enough resolution to distinguish between the magmatic and the hydrothermal system12,31. The recent development of nodal technologies allows the investigation of highly scattering systems with a great resolution32–34. To understand what may have driven the 2021 Vulcano unrest, we deployed a nodal network of 196 sensors across Vulcano and Lipari islands (Fig. 1C).

In this work, we harness the capabilities of a deep neural network to facilitate the automatic and rapid recovery of extensive seismic dispersion data, conducting a Neural Network Nodal Ambient Noise Tomography (N3ANT) of Vulcano. This endeavor aims to investigate the seismic S-wave velocity structure of a volcanic system under unrest, with the objective of understanding its nature and improving the volcanic hazard assessment in the region. Our findings reveal how tectonic and volcanic processes interact and suggest that fault dynamics may trigger volcanic unrest.

---

## Results

We present the 3-D S-wave velocity model of Vulcano retrieved from the N3ANT workflow. As detailed in the Supplementary Methods, N3ANT leverages a deep neural network to harvest nodal array dispersion data from depth-sensitive Rayleigh waves, which dominate virtual seismograms estimated from ambient noise cross-correlation. These data are inverted using a two-step inversion scheme to retrieve the 3-D S-wave velocity model. This involves nonlinear 2-D travel-time tomography inversions35 that are followed by a trans-dimensional Markov chain Monte Carlo (McMC) probabilistic search algorithm36 for 1-D depth inversions. The 3-D S-wave velocity model is shown by means of horizontal (Fig. 2) and vertical (Figs. 3–4) sections. The traces of the vertical sections are indicated in Fig. 2A, and the main anomalies are distinguished between high (H) and low (L) velocity anomalies. A detailed interpretation of each anomaly mentioned below is provided in the Supplementary Discussion and summarized in the Supplementary Table 1. Additionally, the 3-D S-wave velocity model is shown by mean of the Supplementary Movie 1.

Ray-path density maps (Supplementary Fig. 1), combined with a noise directivity analysis (Supplementary Fig. 2A), synthetic resolution tests (Supplementary Figs. 3–6) and a depth-sensitivity analysis (Supplementary Fig. 14), demonstrate the capacity of our network configuration to retrieve reliable information up to 2 km depth. Maximum resolution is reached within the upper first kilometer, below which it starts to decrease and becomes poor below 2 km. Note that the lower resolution achieved in the northern parts of the model allows to spatially detect the anomalies, but prevents the systematic resolution of their precise geometry. For sake of clarity and to avoid drawing interpretations on poorly resolved areas, we combine ray-path density (Supplementary Fig. 1), synthetic tests (Supplementary Figs. 3–6), and depth-sensitivity (Supplementary Fig. 14) information to remove parts of the 3-D model in our illustrations (Supplementary Methods section).

The S-wave velocity model of Vulcano shows La Fossa surrounded in all azimuths by low-velocity zones (L3 in Figs. 2A–B, 3, and 4) that largely fill the caldera between 0 and ~1 km b.s.l., and extend towards the northwest and southeast of the velocity model. These anomalies are overlying and connected to NE-striking, sub-vertical, low-velocity regions (L2 in Figs. 2C–E, 3, and 4), which originate from the bottom of the velocity model at 2 km b.s.l. and are located below the northwestern and southeastern extremities of La Fossa cone. High-velocity anomalies (H2 and H3 in Figs. 2, 3, and 4) are observed from near-surface to greater depths along the rims of La Fossa caldera, respectively located along the eastern (il Piano-Mt. Rosso-Mt. Lucia) and western (Mt. Saraceno-Mt. Lentia-Porto di Ponente) rim. At greater depths, between 1 and 2 km b.s.l., a large and elongated high-velocity region (H1 in Figs. 2C–E, 3, and 4) is observed centered below La Fossa cone. This anomaly appears to be connected to H2 and to H3, respectively below the eastern and western rim of La Fossa caldera (Figs. 2C–E and 3A,C,E). However, the sub-vertical L2 regions (Figs. 2C–E, 3A,B,D, and 4) seem to interrupt these connections, effectively offsetting this large high-velocity domain (H1+H2+H3) into distinct anomalies. One high-velocity anomaly (H4 in Figs. 2C–E and 4) is observed below the southernmost part of Lipari, between 1 and 2 km b.s.l. This anomaly is offset from those below Vulcano by a noticeably large sub-vertical low-velocity region (L1 in Figs. 2, 3A, and 4), which, like the L2 anomalies, originates from the bottom of the velocity model at 2 km b.s.l. and is located below the Bocche di Vulcano region between Lipari and Vulcanello.

The velocity of seismic shear waves is sensitive to several physical attributes such as, among others, stress conditions, porosity, permeability, and pore fluid content, which in turn strongly depend on water saturation, temperature and confining pressure37–40. While the elastic properties of rocks hosting active hydrothermal systems differ from unaltered conditions16, fractured and fluid-saturated regions exhibit lower S-wave velocities (Vs)37,41–43 compared to their intact protoliths. Volcanoes with low Vs usually reflect the presence of (mixed sea/meteoric, magmatic brines and/or hydrothermal) fluid-filled pores and/or partial melts37–40,44–46, as well as fractured units and unconsolidated shallow volcanoclastic deposits40,44,46–48. In short, discriminating among the physical state of fluids solely based on Vs is non-unique and statements would be speculative, which applies to the proposed interpretation.

The N3ANT model is in agreement with previous local earthquake tomographies31,49 (LET) acquired at Vulcano and neighboring regions. At the regional scale, the Vs model supports the separation of Vulcano into two distinct regions, namely the southern high and northern low Vs sectors49. At the local scale, this separation remains consistent but a disagreement is observed at shallow depths (<1 km). The central portion of La Fossa cone and Vulcanello are marked by low Vs (L3 anomalies in Figs. 2A–B and 3), where the local scale LET features high P-wave velocity (Vp) anomalies31. Discrepancies between N3ANT and LET models lie in the parameterization of the inverse problem and the type of wave energy (surface and body waves, respectively) employed for the tomography. Nonetheless, N3ANT offers higher lateral resolution than LET at shallow depths due to the dense ray-path coverage of surface waves (Supplementary Fig. 1) made possible by the large number of stations and the homogeneous distribution of noise sources (Supplementary Fig. 2A). In addition, our acquisition occurred during a volcanic unrest, when increased advective fluid flow characterizes the upper portion of the volcanic edifice. The combination of rising fluids (which condense and percolate through the cone) and hydrothermal circulation of sea and meteoric waters through the loose and permeable infills of La Fossa is expected to lower Vs beneath the volcanic structure. In fact, time-lapse tomography studies have shown the highly transient nature of plumbing systems50, which justifies the differences observed from tomographies decades apart.

Further comparisons can be drawn from a magnetotelluric (MT) model12 acquired during our experiment. The MT model reveals an elongated resistive structure below La Fossa surrounded by shallow conductive zones. This aligns with the Vs model, which shows a system articulated by a broad low-velocity domain within La Fossa caldera, overlaying a large high-velocity region culminating at ~1 km depth (L3, and H1–3 anomalies in Figs. 2A–B and 3A–C and E). The presence of cooled magmatic intrusions is often interpreted from high seismic velocities51 coinciding with high resistivity40,52–54, while seismic velocities in association with high conductivity suggest fracturing along with (hydrothermal) fluid circulation and alteration47,55,56.

Observations made by geothermal exploration wells (Fig. 1C) also strongly support our Vs model. For instance, the L2 and L3 anomalies located on Baia di Levante marks the hydrothermal alteration and hot steam discharges at shallow depths (~200∘C at ~200 m b.s.l.) evidenced by the VU1 and VU2 wells57–59. The Vulcano Porto well (VP1) indicates a convection-conduction transition boundary (between shallow permeable rocks and deep impermeable lavas) at ~600 m b.s.l., and sub-volcanic bodies at the maximum depth of 1’000 m12,58. While the transition boundary remains undetected due to the strong low-velocity intensity of the L2 and L3 anomalies, the 1 km deep sub-horizontal roof delineated by the observed high-velocity anomalies (Figs. 3 and 4) fit the first occurrence of intrusive bodies seen in the well. This further aligns and is supported by ~300 concurrent VLP events, which remained spatially quasi-stationary throughout their monitoring period14. The average VLP hypocenter has a depth of ~0.85±0.23 km b.s.l.14, which falls at the L2–L3 anomalies’ interface (Figs. 3A and 4). The Isola di Vulcano well (IV1) penetrated a monzodioritic intrusion at 1.36 km depth60, which was also detected by the local-scale LET31. The H3 anomaly fits the detection of this intrusion below Grotta dei Palizzi (Fig. 3D).

Figure 4 shows the conceptual model we propose for the shallow plumbing system of Vulcano superimposed on a vertical section of the S-wave velocity 3-D model. This section is sub-parallel to the ATLF and connects the southernmost part of Lipari to il Piano across the sites of Vucanello, Baia di Levante, and La Fossa. All anomalies mentioned above are shown, as well as the locations of key wells57,58 and the average VLP hypocenter14. Our model does not require the shallow emplacement of new batches of magma, although we cannot exclude the occurrence of ancient melts ponding at shallow depths22,61. For instance, the L1 and L2 anomalies show Vs values as low as 1 km s−1, which may be compatible with melts (e.g., magma, mush, etc.). However, they are also compatible with a fluid-rich and highly fractured region or with a more ductile rheology, such as a crystallizing domain where fluids are not as mobile as in a freshly emplaced melt.

We propose a key role of local tectonics in driving unrest and argue, in agreement with previous authors, that the ATLF is a right-lateral NW-striking transtensional fault along which the Vulcano-Lipari-Salina volcanism develops1,2,4,62. ### Reviewer 3

This manuscript presents a detailed study of the Vulcano volcanic system using Nodal Ambient Noise Tomography (NANT)
to reveal the subsurface structure during volcanic unrest. The study is timely and relevant given the recent activity of the
volcano and its potential hazard to surrounding populations. However, while the application of NANT is robust, there are
several points regarding the methodology, results, and overall contribution that require further clarification. Below are
specific comments and suggestions for improvement.
Detailed Comments:
• Line 208: The connection between the bandpass filter and the assumption of group velocity and array aperture is unclear.
Could you explain how these factors are related?
• Line 240: What criteria were used to re-extract the 557 dispersion curves? Please provide a clear explanation to justify this
decision.
• Figure S1: The period for the ray path density map is not specified. Please clarify which period this map represents to
provide a clearer understanding of the data coverage.
• Figure S2: In panel B, many early arrivals before the 2 km/s threshold suggest the noise sources may be unevenly
distributed. Could this non-uniform distribution affect the accuracy of your dispersion measurements? If so, please discuss
how it might influence the results.
• Figures S3 and S4: There are visible artifacts in the northern and southern parts of the inversion results, where the
resolution appears to be poor. These areas should either be removed from the model or flagged as regions with low
confidence.
• Coordinate Systems (Figures S3, S4, and 2): There is an inconsistency in the coordinate systems used (Lat/Lon in Figures
S3 and S4 vs. UTM in Figure 2), which makes it difficult to assess and compare the resolution of the model. Please use a
consistent coordinate system throughout the manuscript.
• Figure S6: The caption does not provide sufficient information for panels B, C, and D. If these panels are not explained, it
may be better to remove them. Additionally, for panel A, how was the white line generated?
• Figure S7: The parameters for Vp, Vs, layer thickness, and density are not well explained. What were these values, and
what is the rationale for selecting them? Please justify the choices made in this figure.
Additional Suggestions:
1. Novelty and Contribution:
While the paper offers valuable insights into the subsurface structure of Vulcano during unrest, the methodological
innovation appears limited. The study primarily employs well-established techniques using existing open-source algorithms
for processing and inversion. To strengthen the paper’s impact, I recommend emphasizing any new developments in the
approach or highlighting how this methodology can be applied to other volcanic systems. The application of deep learning
for automated dispersion curve extraction is notable but should be further discussed in terms of its broader implications.
2. Significance of the Sub-Horizontal Magmatic Intrusion:
One of the key findings is the identification of a sub-horizontal magmatic intrusion at 1.5 km depth. This could represent a
significant contribution to the understanding of Vulcano’s magmatic plumbing system. However, I would recommend
providing more context about how this discovery advances existing models of volcanic unrest and whether similar structures
have been identified in other volcanic systems. This would help position the study within a global context and enhance its
relevance.
3. Broader Implications for Volcanic Hazard Mitigation:
The study highlights the potential for using NANT to inform hazard mitigation strategies. However, the discussion on how
this method could be operationalized in real-time volcanic monitoring is underdeveloped. I suggest expanding on how this
technique could be rapidly implemented during periods of volcanic unrest to aid decision-making and potentially prevent
disasters.
4. Uncertainty and Limitations:
The manuscript could benefit from a more thorough discussion of the uncertainties and limitations of the study. For example,
the poor resolution in certain areas, as seen in Figures S3 and S4, should be explicitly addressed. Moreover, considering
the non-uniform distribution of noise sources, the potential impact on the accuracy of the dispersion curves should be
discussed.
5. Integration with Other Geophysical Data:
While the study focuses on ambient noise tomography, integrating additional geophysical methods, such as
magnetotellurics, gravity, or resistivity, could provide a more comprehensive understanding of the subsurface structure.
I encourage the authors to explore the possibility of using these complementary data sources to validate or enhance their
findings.
Overall, this study provides valuable insights into the subsurface structure of Vulcano during unrest. However, the
manuscript could benefit from clearer explanations of the methods, a more in-depth discussion of the findings’ broader
implications, and addressing some inconsistencies and limitations in the results. Improving these areas will enhance the
manuscript’s scientific contribution and potential impact.

### Reviewer 4

Review of “Imaging volcanoes during unrest: Ambient Noise Tomography of a transient plumbing system, Vulcano, Italy.” by Stumpp et al., submitted to Nature: Communications.

Overview and Impact:
This work provides a novel isotropic S-wave velocity model of the volcanic structure under Volcano Island using surface wave dispersion curves obtained from Ambient Noise. Dispersion curves were obtained from data recorded at a novel high-N (≈ 200 ) nodal seismic array deployed at the volcano using advanced deep neural network strategies. The final Bayesian MCMC inversion leads to a preferred velocity model that is interpreted with available geophysical and geological/volcanological data in terms of the volcano's deep structures, leading to unrest.

It is daunting to describe so many recording sites and the corresponding data processing. The authors use a rigorous and very robust approach for dispersion curve quality selection, exploiting recent advancements in deep neural networks. The overall preliminary work on the data is at an excellent standard. The figures are of exceptional quality, especially Figs. 1 and 3, which provides the necessary framework to interpret the results. Fig. 4 represents a clear, high-impact view of the structures and processes interpreted by the authors under Volcano. The interpretation is based on the most recent research regarding Volcano’s unrest, which is skillfully used by the study and explains nicely trade-offs between deformation and previous seismic models. Nature: Communications is an appropriate outlet for such a work, considering the many high-impact works published on this topic by the journal through the last decade.

We present several critical comments, which are divided into Technique and Interpretation (which includes representation). Additional comments can be followed at the discretion of the authors in case they can improve the flow of the paper and correct Typos. If published, the paper would be highly impactful, providing much-needed data on the deep volcanic structure and processes. We can only provide sufficient expertise to review the seismology used by the study, evaluate the reliability of the volcanological interpretation, and assess the general quality/impact of the study. However, the results might become a standard for the understanding/interpretation of volcanic processes at Volcano. For this reason, we highly recommend a revision from a volcanologist expert in the processes acting under the volcano.

In Summary, we answer the primary questions proposed to reviewers by this journal as follows:
- What are the noteworthy results? Any work using seismological data from massive arrays like this is remarkable and valuable. The selection process in a volcanic environment is extremely challenging and addressed very well by the study. The interpretation of the results is grounded on very extended literature and a relevant amount of volcanological data and experience. The retrieved connection between the volcanic systems of Lipari and Volcano, with its deep source under the second, represents an important result for our understanding of the two volcanic systems.
- Will the work be of significance to the field and related fields? How does it compare to the established literature? If the work is not original, please provide relevant references. The work is original and represents an important improvement relative to the current geophysical understanding of the volcano.
- Does the work support the conclusions and claims, or is additional evidence needed? Further evidence is required in order to support all the work’s claims.
- Are there any flaws in the data analysis, interpretation and conclusions? - Do these prohibit publication or require revision? None of the flaws in data analysis, interpretation and conclusions we found forbid publication, but they require revision.
- Is the methodology sound? Does the work meet the expected standards in your field?
The methodology of the current study requires further work and clarifications to meet the standard in our field.
- Is there enough detail provided in the methods for the work to be reproduced? The details provided are currently insufficient.

Critical Comments:
1) Technique
a) 2-D group-velocity maps:
While the processing and quality assessment of dispersion curves are excellent, the technical description of how they obtain 2-D group velocity maps lacks clarity and details:
1. The only paper mentioned is [54], but the reader cannot rely only on that. The authors should say more about the experimental assumptions they make. For example, do they take into account finite frequencies, or do they use ray theory to describe wave propagation? They mention a "Nonlinear inversion", but it is not clear what they are referring to. If they use ray theory, does it mean that they take ray bending into account? Assuming ray theory, what algorithm do they use for forward modelling? Do they solve the Eikonal with the Fast Marching/Sweeping Method, or do they use a Shortest Path Network? Despite the sharpness required by the journal, it is their job to clarify these points.
2. The authors talk about refinements of the parameterisation (i.e., discretisation?), but they do not say anything about the type of basis functions they use. Do they use pixels? Do they use splines or sines/cosines? What does this refinement of the parameterisation consist of? Is it done a priori based on the coverage? Showing a figure to clarify is necessary.
3. The 1. authors do not discuss the inversion method. We guess they use an iterative approach with linearisation at each step, like the Gauss-Newton or Levemberg–Marquardt method. If this is the case, do they use some regularisation (Norm vs roughness damping.)? If it is roughness damping, do they use the first or second derivative of the model? How did they select the damping?
4. More generally, while the paper [54], developed by Cabrera-Peréz, is a starting point, it remains a theoretical paper that starts from concepts applied to the nonlinear inversion of seismic refraction profiles. To understand its full reliability, the authors must accurately develop and describe the model and approximations within this study, especially in the Supplementary Materials. For example, the authors use a test for „scales“ without clearly defining what this scale is: as it is, it appears redundant with Fig S3. Only by reading previous literature can one guess that in the case of Fig S4, scale is (maybe!) node parametrisation. The reader is supposed to get all the information necessary here without having to guess the steps that have led to the results.
5. The scale is selected based on 0.02º x 0.02º anomalies (Fig. S4), but the entire workflow and all results are interpreted at a resolution of 0.01º x 0.01º. This is inappropriate, and assessing with 0.01º x 0.01º is central to understanding eventual trade-offs in the increasing parametrisation strategy used by the inversion.
6. We need to understand why a single checkerboard test is shown for the group velocities (Fig. S3). The authors use five periods between 0.5 s and 2.5 s: the period is not declared for Fig. S3, and no resolution assessment is made for the other periods. Does the previous selection criteria require the same source station pairs to be available at all periods? This could be the explanation, but it would reduce the number of available data without reason.

b) Vs model (MCMC inversion):
We also have critical comments about the final Vs inversion:
1. The authors use a Bayesian inversion, but they do not show the resulting uncertainty anywhere.
2. We do not understand what their favourite model is. Is it the ensemble mean or the median? How far apart are the mean and median? Typically (certainly in our experience), when the mean and median are quite far apart, it indicates that some Markov chains are stuck in some region of the parameter space associated with a relatively high (low) likelihood (misfit) that is not associated with a sensible earth model. For example, high velocities at shallow depths and low velocities at depths can produce low misfits in the inversion of surface-wave dispersion curves. Still, such a 1D model needs to make sense geophysically, even within complex volcanic structures.
3. Regarding the Bayesian sampling, we need to understand how many models the authors save (among the accepted ones) in the iterations after the burn-in. This information is important because keeping all the accepted models in a perturbative approach (where each proposed model is proposed by randomly perturbing the last accepted model) means having a final ensemble that is highly autocorrelated, which goes against the Bayesian paradigm, whereby the various models that compose the ensemble are independent of each other.
4. To mitigate this autocorrelation problem, most Bayesian sampling software saves one model for every N accepted models. BayHunter does it differently: it saves them all, and at the end of the inversion, it selects a random subset of the ensemble. This generally works fine; however, the authors only run ~17,300 iterations after burn-in, which means that the randomly selected subset could still be affected by autocorrelations. Given this, we suggest increasing the number of iterations after burn-in to at least 100k total iterations.

2) Interpretation
a) Assessment and Figures
The paper's figures are of high quality and very well crafted; however, they do not consider the results of the checkerboard testing accurately, and novel synthetic tests appear necessary when interpreting features. This adds to our concerns about testing different group velocity maps for various periods.
1. The checkerboard tests are shown for horizontal sections and different periods, but parts of the areas cannot be recovered adequately. These parts are still present in the S-wave velocity maps (Fig. 2) and are sometimes interpreted. Fig. 2 should report only areas where the velocity model can be reconstructed at a level allowing interpretation (thus at a minimum of 0.01º x 0.01º), Fig. S3F. The shading on unresolved areas should consider the results of testing scales for 0.01º x 0.01º checkerboard anomalies.
2. Fig. 4 will be indubitably the one the majority of readers will remember, sparking interpretations about the volcanoes from different disciplines. This figure must better acknowledge resolution issues. Volumes below 2.5 km are defined as those where resolution is maximum and then starts to decrease: we strongly disagree. If looking at Fig. S7, only periods of 2.5 s (primarily) and 2 s (partially) have any sensitivity at this depth. Resolutions on the volumes below this depth might not even be at a scale of 0.02º x 0.02º. The authors effectively have no way to assess if the contrast observed in Figure S5 at 2 s is real with the current materials. The contrast is strongly dampened at 2.5 s. It is necessary to shade any volume below this depth for all figures, certainly avoiding drawing any interpreted feature in Figure 4 below this depth.
3. Anomalies H1 and H4 are both in the northern part of the study area, where resolution testing is negative. The two H1 anomalies have quite an important role in the interpretation [Lines 121-139]. Still, at present, its recovery cannot be considered reliable, even less its description as a spherical anomaly and, consequently, its interpretation. A spike test of the corresponding dimension could better prove its reliability. The authors only note H4 as it corresponds to the high velocities of [42], so its lack of recovery is not as problematic, but the lack of resolution should be acknowledged in the text. A second spike test would better clarify the resolution.
4. While L1 can be recovered in the resolved depth span, we recommend a wider synthetic test of L1 at all periods considered. This would provide stronger evidence that L2, and especially the low-velocity pathway connecting to Lipary through Vulcanello, are no ghosts.

b) Interpreted features
Here, we discuss interpreted features, highlighting where we find inconsistencies.
1. Throughout the paper, the authors make no mention of high-velocity anomalies that might correspond to crater rims. Velocity tomography (Di Stefano et al., 2002; Vanorio et al., 2005; Battaglia et al., 2008), including ANT results (De Siena et al, 2018) show that high-velocity shallow anomalies (< 1.5 km) like those recovered around L1 are the buried trace of such rims at 1 km (Figs. 2 and 3): the correlation with the crater rims shown in Fig, 1 of H2 and H3 supports this interpretation. This interpretation would greatly simplify the discussion and fit with the conclusions and discussions better than what is currently proposed.
2. The break in the high-velocity continuity around L1 in the NNW can be due to the collapsed caldera collapse, as discussed by the authors. In this case, we need to understand the role of H1. Are the authors claiming these anomalies are a signature of supercritical fluids? Are they a remnant of past intrusions? Suppose the anomalies can be resolved separately (see previous point). In that case, do we see them as forming a caprock for low-velocity fluids feeding Baia di Levante (see, e.g., Vanorio & Kanitpanyacharoen, 2015), as suggested by the „Sealing cap“ in Fig. 4 (but never mentioned in the text? Lines 121-139 should better clarify the geochemistry of the fluids involved, making the interpretation of the S-wave velocity anomaly unclear. From our experience, such an interpretation is challenging without measurements of Vp/Vs (Vanorio et al., 2005; Vanorio & Kanitpanyacharoen, 2015).
3. Line 171: Throughout the paper, the authors are very loose in the description of what magma is for them. Here, they write “The top of the magma is hypothesized.. “ What magma? A body, a sill, a mush? More generally, this is a problem in the text that could come back to bite from petrologists experts of the magma system. The interpretation of a low-velocity anomaly using Vs values is considered weak. The strength of having the anomaly correctly explaining both deformation and VLP models is indubitable. However, the work can be attacked without a correct petrophysical explanation of what type of magma is interpreted. Using current literature and petrological observations, such as those done by Jaxybulatov et al. (2014), appears crucial to mitigate criticisms.

3) Additional comments
a) The authors could specify if they add noise to their synthetics.
b) It could be more elegant to avoid the use of code lines in equations: the authors could use a mathematic one instead of VarRed in Eq. 1.
c) Abstract: “entered in unrest” or “entered into unrest”
d) Abstract: “and help discriminateing” as it still refers to “can”.
e) Line 168: We strongly advise against this sentence, which reduces the study's impact. The fact that it agrees with previous studies is likely not the concept the authors want to express; it is that the model resolves apparent contradictions between different interpretations of seismic and deformation models.
f) Adding the additional references in this review is not necessary for publication: they are only mentioned to clarify our points.

Best Wishes,
Luca De Siena and Fabrizio Magrini

Given the broader significance outlined in the abstract and conclusions, reframing this goal could add impact. ### Reviewer 1

We congratulate the authors for thoroughly addressing our comments from the first review. The paper has improved
significantly, both technically and interpretively, and fulfils its initial technical and high-impact promises. Our initial review
was very extensive and we feel the effort to respond and honesty of the responses is commendable. The work is now at a
very high standard: we are particularly impressed by the volcanological implications of the results.
However, after these changes, we still have one major technical concern. If this issue is resolved, we strongly support the
publication of this work.
Our concern pertains to Fig. S9 in the supplementary materials. The probability density of the shear wave velocity profile
appears very rough. As the authors illustrate in the histogram (panel c), the chosen data noise is exceptionally low. We
understand that they use a standard deviation for the uniform prior ranging from 1x10^5 to 1x10-3: is this true? Even the
maximum is very low, translating to Vs/1000 for Vs=3 km/s. This leads to overfitting, which is evident in the rough histogram
in panel a. One can employ such a small standard deviation, but more than 100 iterations are required to sample the
posterior. Such a posterior appears undersampled.
The solution is to increase the maximum standard deviation in the inversion to 10-1, a value that will produce a much
smoother posterior and greater, yet more reliable, uncertainty. The robustness must be tested following this procedure, as
we are also discussing volcanic media, where uncertainties are higher than at regional and continental scales. Since this is
the only figure presented by the authors, we infer that it represents one of the best-case scenarios.
Best Wishes,
Luca De Siena and Fabrizio Magrini

## Paper

## Abstract

Volcanic risk escalates significantly during unrest. In late 2021, the Italian island of Vulcano entered into a phase of unrest featuring Very Long Period seismic events, which are considered to be markers of magma and gas flowing across the volcanic plumbing system. Here we show how Neural Network Nodal Ambient Noise Tomography generates a high-resolution shear-wave velocity model for investigating the causative drivers of Vulcano’s unrest. Using a deep learning model we harvest seismic dispersion data from a dense nodal seismic network deployed during the early unrest’s phase. The inverted 3-D model reveals a high-resolution tomography of the shallow part of a volcanic system in unrest. If deployed and rapidly processed in (near) real-time during periods of unrest, Neural Network Nodal Ambient Noise Tomography can lead to dynamic and adaptive evacuation plans. Such advances would contribute to more effective, source-dependent risk mitigation schemes in volcanic regions, potentially saving lives.

---

## Introduction

The island of Vulcano, along with Lipari and Salina, constitutes the central volcanic ridge of the Aeolian archipelago on the Tyrrhenian Sea, southern Italy (Fig. 1A). This central sector is aligned with the NNW-SSE regional Aeolian-Tindari-Letojanni (ATLF) strike-slip fault system1–4 (Fig. 1A–B). Vulcano experienced multiple Vulcanian-style eruptions with frequent transitions from magmatic to phreatomagmatic activity5, and has remained quiescent since its last eruption in 1888-1890 AD. However, below La Fossa caldera (Fig. 1C), the primary volcanic feature of Vulcano, an active hydrothermal system at a depth of between 0.5 and 1 km below sea level (b.s.l.)6–8 has been intermittently affected by episodic inputs of magmatic fluids and volcanic degassing unrest over the past four decades9,10. Considering the importance of the island for tourists, the exposure to volcanic hazards remains exceedingly high even for minor eruptive events or episodes of increased degassing3,11,12.

Since early September 2021, La Fossa caldera exhibited increased activity characterized by a rapid intensification of previously unseen unrest indicators8,12–16. This activity was marked by a large rate of increase in fumarolic temperatures, accompanied by substantial emissions of CO2-rich and SO2 magmatic gases and diffuse soil fluxes8,10,13,14,16. A centimeter-scale uplift was also observed at La Fossa, along with a significant increase of local seismicity, and the detection of Very Long Period (VLP) seismic signals8,14–16. VLPs are a distinctive feature of this unrest as they are usually attributed to the release of magma and/or pressurized magmatic fluids through the shallow fractured volcanic conduits12,14,16–18. Although the unrest phase is no longer at its peak, and the yellow alert level declared by the Italian Civil Protection on October 1st 2021 was set back to green on December 19th 202319, an increase in VLP events, fumaroles temperatures and gas emissions was detected again starting from May 202420. The current unrest shares similarities with Vulcano’s previous crisis of the late 1970s to early 1990s16, suggesting that the current episode may continue for several more years21.

The latest conceptual models discussing this unrest suggest either the persistent degassing, at a reduced rate, of a deep-seated magmatic source at about 4-5 km depth8, or increased activity of the shallow hydrothermal system16,21. In the past, some authors proposed the replenishment of the shallow hydrothermal system with magmatic fluids originating from the pulsating degassing process of a deeper, pressurized, and stationary magmatic body5,7–9,11–14,22,23. Nonetheless, Vulcano’s plumbing system is believed to be a polybaric intricate magmatic network with reservoirs having sill and dike-like structures8,11,22. Unfortunately, the geophysical data are sparse and mainly constrained by airborne geophysics24–27. Onshore studies do not penetrate enough in the plumbing system to reveal the interplay between magmatic and hydrothermal fluids28–30. Only recent investigations have shown the plumbing system down to a few kilometers depth but none of them had enough resolution to distinguish between the magmatic and the hydrothermal system12,31. The recent development of nodal technologies allows the investigation of highly scattering systems with a great resolution32–34. To understand what may have driven the 2021 Vulcano unrest, we deployed a nodal network of 196 sensors across Vulcano and Lipari islands (Fig. 1C).

In this work, we harness the capabilities of a deep neural network to facilitate the automatic and rapid recovery of extensive seismic dispersion data, conducting a Neural Network Nodal Ambient Noise Tomography (N3ANT) of Vulcano. This endeavor aims to investigate the seismic S-wave velocity structure of a volcanic system under unrest, with the objective of understanding its nature and improving the volcanic hazard assessment in the region. Our findings reveal how tectonic and volcanic processes interact and suggest that fault dynamics may trigger volcanic unrest.

---

## Results

We present the 3-D S-wave velocity model of Vulcano retrieved from the N3ANT workflow. As detailed in the Supplementary Methods, N3ANT leverages a deep neural network to harvest nodal array dispersion data from depth-sensitive Rayleigh waves, which dominate virtual seismograms estimated from ambient noise cross-correlation. These data are inverted using a two-step inversion scheme to retrieve the 3-D S-wave velocity model. This involves nonlinear 2-D travel-time tomography inversions35 that are followed by a trans-dimensional Markov chain Monte Carlo (McMC) probabilistic search algorithm36 for 1-D depth inversions. The 3-D S-wave velocity model is shown by means of horizontal (Fig. 2) and vertical (Figs. 3–4) sections. The traces of the vertical sections are indicated in Fig. 2A, and the main anomalies are distinguished between high (H) and low (L) velocity anomalies. A detailed interpretation of each anomaly mentioned below is provided in the Supplementary Discussion and summarized in the Supplementary Table 1. Additionally, the 3-D S-wave velocity model is shown by mean of the Supplementary Movie 1.

Ray-path density maps (Supplementary Fig. 1), combined with a noise directivity analysis (Supplementary Fig. 2A), synthetic resolution tests (Supplementary Figs. 3–6) and a depth-sensitivity analysis (Supplementary Fig. 14), demonstrate the capacity of our network configuration to retrieve reliable information up to 2 km depth. Maximum resolution is reached within the upper first kilometer, below which it starts to decrease and becomes poor below 2 km. Note that the lower resolution achieved in the northern parts of the model allows to spatially detect the anomalies, but prevents the systematic resolution of their precise geometry. For sake of clarity and to avoid drawing interpretations on poorly resolved areas, we combine ray-path density (Supplementary Fig. 1), synthetic tests (Supplementary Figs. 3–6), and depth-sensitivity (Supplementary Fig. 14) information to remove parts of the 3-D model in our illustrations (Supplementary Methods section).

The S-wave velocity model of Vulcano shows La Fossa surrounded in all azimuths by low-velocity zones (L3 in Figs. 2A–B, 3, and 4) that largely fill the caldera between 0 and ~1 km b.s.l., and extend towards the northwest and southeast of the velocity model. These anomalies are overlying and connected to NE-striking, sub-vertical, low-velocity regions (L2 in Figs. 2C–E, 3, and 4), which originate from the bottom of the velocity model at 2 km b.s.l. and are located below the northwestern and southeastern extremities of La Fossa cone. High-velocity anomalies (H2 and H3 in Figs. 2, 3, and 4) are observed from near-surface to greater depths along the rims of La Fossa caldera, respectively located along the eastern (il Piano-Mt. Rosso-Mt. Lucia) and western (Mt. Saraceno-Mt. Lentia-Porto di Ponente) rim. At greater depths, between 1 and 2 km b.s.l., a large and elongated high-velocity region (H1 in Figs. 2C–E, 3, and 4) is observed centered below La Fossa cone. This anomaly appears to be connected to H2 and to H3, respectively below the eastern and western rim of La Fossa caldera (Figs. 2C–E and 3A,C,E). However, the sub-vertical L2 regions (Figs. 2C–E, 3A,B,D, and 4) seem to interrupt these connections, effectively offsetting this large high-velocity domain (H1+H2+H3) into distinct anomalies. One high-velocity anomaly (H4 in Figs. 2C–E and 4) is observed below the southernmost part of Lipari, between 1 and 2 km b.s.l. This anomaly is offset from those below Vulcano by a noticeably large sub-vertical low-velocity region (L1 in Figs. 2, 3A, and 4), which, like the L2 anomalies, originates from the bottom of the velocity model at 2 km b.s.l. and is located below the Bocche di Vulcano region between Lipari and Vulcanello.

The velocity of seismic shear waves is sensitive to several physical attributes such as, among others, stress conditions, porosity, permeability, and pore fluid content, which in turn strongly depend on water saturation, temperature and confining pressure37–40. While the elastic properties of rocks hosting active hydrothermal systems differ from unaltered conditions16, fractured and fluid-saturated regions exhibit lower S-wave velocities (Vs)37,41–43 compared to their intact protoliths. Volcanoes with low Vs usually reflect the presence of (mixed sea/meteoric, magmatic brines and/or hydrothermal) fluid-filled pores and/or partial melts37–40,44–46, as well as fractured units and unconsolidated shallow volcanoclastic deposits40,44,46–48. In short, discriminating among the physical state of fluids solely based on Vs is non-unique and statements would be speculative, which applies to the proposed interpretation.

The N3ANT model is in agreement with previous local earthquake tomographies31,49 (LET) acquired at Vulcano and neighboring regions. At the regional scale, the Vs model supports the separation of Vulcano into two distinct regions, namely the southern high and northern low Vs sectors49. At the local scale, this separation remains consistent but a disagreement is observed at shallow depths (<1 km). The central portion of La Fossa cone and Vulcanello are marked by low Vs (L3 anomalies in Figs. 2A–B and 3), where the local scale LET features high P-wave velocity (Vp) anomalies31. Discrepancies between N3ANT and LET models lie in the parameterization of the inverse problem and the type of wave energy (surface and body waves, respectively) employed for the tomography. Nonetheless, N3ANT offers higher lateral resolution than LET at shallow depths due to the dense ray-path coverage of surface waves (Supplementary Fig. 1) made possible by the large number of stations and the homogeneous distribution of noise sources (Supplementary Fig. 2A). In addition, our acquisition occurred during a volcanic unrest, when increased advective fluid flow characterizes the upper portion of the volcanic edifice. The combination of rising fluids (which condense and percolate through the cone) and hydrothermal circulation of sea and meteoric waters through the loose and permeable infills of La Fossa is expected to lower Vs beneath the volcanic structure. In fact, time-lapse tomography studies have shown the highly transient nature of plumbing systems50, which justifies the differences observed from tomographies decades apart.

Further comparisons can be drawn from a magnetotelluric (MT) model12 acquired during our experiment. The MT model reveals an elongated resistive structure below La Fossa surrounded by shallow conductive zones. This aligns with the Vs model, which shows a system articulated by a broad low-velocity domain within La Fossa caldera, overlaying a large high-velocity region culminating at ~1 km depth (L3, and H1–3 anomalies in Figs. 2A–B and 3A–C and E). The presence of cooled magmatic intrusions is often interpreted from high seismic velocities51 coinciding with high resistivity40,52–54, while seismic velocities in association with high conductivity suggest fracturing along with (hydrothermal) fluid circulation and alteration47,55,56.

Observations made by geothermal exploration wells (Fig. 1C) also strongly support our Vs model. For instance, the L2 and L3 anomalies located on Baia di Levante marks the hydrothermal alteration and hot steam discharges at shallow depths (~200∘C at ~200 m b.s.l.) evidenced by the VU1 and VU2 wells57–59. The Vulcano Porto well (VP1) indicates a convection-conduction transition boundary (between shallow permeable rocks and deep impermeable lavas) at ~600 m b.s.l., and sub-volcanic bodies at the maximum depth of 1’000 m12,58. While the transition boundary remains undetected due to the strong low-velocity intensity of the L2 and L3 anomalies, the 1 km deep sub-horizontal roof delineated by the observed high-velocity anomalies (Figs. 3 and 4) fit the first occurrence of intrusive bodies seen in the well. This further aligns and is supported by ~300 concurrent VLP events, which remained spatially quasi-stationary throughout their monitoring period14. The average VLP hypocenter has a depth of ~0.85±0.23 km b.s.l.14, which falls at the L2–L3 anomalies’ interface (Figs. 3A and 4). The Isola di Vulcano well (IV1) penetrated a monzodioritic intrusion at 1.36 km depth60, which was also detected by the local-scale LET31. The H3 anomaly fits the detection of this intrusion below Grotta dei Palizzi (Fig. 3D).

Figure 4 shows the conceptual model we propose for the shallow plumbing system of Vulcano superimposed on a vertical section of the S-wave velocity 3-D model. This section is sub-parallel to the ATLF and connects the southernmost part of Lipari to il Piano across the sites of Vucanello, Baia di Levante, and La Fossa. All anomalies mentioned above are shown, as well as the locations of key wells57,58 and the average VLP hypocenter14. Our model does not require the shallow emplacement of new batches of magma, although we cannot exclude the occurrence of ancient melts ponding at shallow depths22,61. For instance, the L1 and L2 anomalies show Vs values as low as 1 km s−1, which may be compatible with melts (e.g., magma, mush, etc.). However, they are also compatible with a fluid-rich and highly fractured region or with a more ductile rheology, such as a crystallizing domain where fluids are not as mobile as in a freshly emplaced melt.

We propose a key role of local tectonics in driving unrest and argue, in agreement with previous authors, that the ATLF is a right-lateral NW-striking transtensional fault along which the Vulcano-Lipari-Salina volcanism develops1,2,4,62. ### Reviewer 3

This manuscript presents a detailed study of the Vulcano volcanic system using Nodal Ambient Noise Tomography (NANT)
to reveal the subsurface structure during volcanic unrest. The study is timely and relevant given the recent activity of the
volcano and its potential hazard to surrounding populations. However, while the application of NANT is robust, there are
several points regarding the methodology, results, and overall contribution that require further clarification. Below are
specific comments and suggestions for improvement.
Detailed Comments:
• Line 208: The connection between the bandpass filter and the assumption of group velocity and array aperture is unclear.
Could you explain how these factors are related?
• Line 240: What criteria were used to re-extract the 557 dispersion curves? Please provide a clear explanation to justify this
decision.
• Figure S1: The period for the ray path density map is not specified. Please clarify which period this map represents to
provide a clearer understanding of the data coverage.
• Figure S2: In panel B, many early arrivals before the 2 km/s threshold suggest the noise sources may be unevenly
distributed. Could this non-uniform distribution affect the accuracy of your dispersion measurements? If so, please discuss
how it might influence the results.
• Figures S3 and S4: There are visible artifacts in the northern and southern parts of the inversion results, where the
resolution appears to be poor. These areas should either be removed from the model or flagged as regions with low
confidence.
• Coordinate Systems (Figures S3, S4, and 2): There is an inconsistency in the coordinate systems used (Lat/Lon in Figures
S3 and S4 vs. UTM in Figure 2), which makes it difficult to assess and compare the resolution of the model. Please use a
consistent coordinate system throughout the manuscript.
• Figure S6: The caption does not provide sufficient information for panels B, C, and D. If these panels are not explained, it
may be better to remove them. Additionally, for panel A, how was the white line generated?
• Figure S7: The parameters for Vp, Vs, layer thickness, and density are not well explained. What were these values, and
what is the rationale for selecting them? Please justify the choices made in this figure.
Additional Suggestions:
1. Novelty and Contribution:
While the paper offers valuable insights into the subsurface structure of Vulcano during unrest, the methodological
innovation appears limited. The study primarily employs well-established techniques using existing open-source algorithms
for processing and inversion. To strengthen the paper’s impact, I recommend emphasizing any new developments in the
approach or highlighting how this methodology can be applied to other volcanic systems. The application of deep learning
for automated dispersion curve extraction is notable but should be further discussed in terms of its broader implications.
2. Significance of the Sub-Horizontal Magmatic Intrusion:
One of the key findings is the identification of a sub-horizontal magmatic intrusion at 1.5 km depth. This could represent a
significant contribution to the understanding of Vulcano’s magmatic plumbing system. However, I would recommend
providing more context about how this discovery advances existing models of volcanic unrest and whether similar structures
have been identified in other volcanic systems. This would help position the study within a global context and enhance its
relevance.
3. Broader Implications for Volcanic Hazard Mitigation:
The study highlights the potential for using NANT to inform hazard mitigation strategies. However, the discussion on how
this method could be operationalized in real-time volcanic monitoring is underdeveloped. I suggest expanding on how this
technique could be rapidly implemented during periods of volcanic unrest to aid decision-making and potentially prevent
disasters.
4. Uncertainty and Limitations:
The manuscript could benefit from a more thorough discussion of the uncertainties and limitations of the study. For example,
the poor resolution in certain areas, as seen in Figures S3 and S4, should be explicitly addressed. Moreover, considering
the non-uniform distribution of noise sources, the potential impact on the accuracy of the dispersion curves should be
discussed.
5. Integration with Other Geophysical Data:
While the study focuses on ambient noise tomography, integrating additional geophysical methods, such as
magnetotellurics, gravity, or resistivity, could provide a more comprehensive understanding of the subsurface structure.
I encourage the authors to explore the possibility of using these complementary data sources to validate or enhance their
findings.
Overall, this study provides valuable insights into the subsurface structure of Vulcano during unrest. However, the
manuscript could benefit from clearer explanations of the methods, a more in-depth discussion of the findings’ broader
implications, and addressing some inconsistencies and limitations in the results. Improving these areas will enhance the
manuscript’s scientific contribution and potential impact.

### Reviewer 4

Review of “Imaging volcanoes during unrest: Ambient Noise Tomography of a transient plumbing system, Vulcano, Italy.” by Stumpp et al., submitted to Nature: Communications.

Overview and Impact:
This work provides a novel isotropic S-wave velocity model of the volcanic structure under Volcano Island using surface wave dispersion curves obtained from Ambient Noise. Dispersion curves were obtained from data recorded at a novel high-N (≈ 200 ) nodal seismic array deployed at the volcano using advanced deep neural network strategies. The final Bayesian MCMC inversion leads to a preferred velocity model that is interpreted with available geophysical and geological/volcanological data in terms of the volcano's deep structures, leading to unrest.

It is daunting to describe so many recording sites and the corresponding data processing. The authors use a rigorous and very robust approach for dispersion curve quality selection, exploiting recent advancements in deep neural networks. The overall preliminary work on the data is at an excellent standard. The figures are of exceptional quality, especially Figs. 1 and 3, which provides the necessary framework to interpret the results. Fig. 4 represents a clear, high-impact view of the structures and processes interpreted by the authors under Volcano. The interpretation is based on the most recent research regarding Volcano’s unrest, which is skillfully used by the study and explains nicely trade-offs between deformation and previous seismic models. Nature: Communications is an appropriate outlet for such a work, considering the many high-impact works published on this topic by the journal through the last decade.

We present several critical comments, which are divided into Technique and Interpretation (which includes representation). Additional comments can be followed at the discretion of the authors in case they can improve the flow of the paper and correct Typos. If published, the paper would be highly impactful, providing much-needed data on the deep volcanic structure and processes. We can only provide sufficient expertise to review the seismology used by the study, evaluate the reliability of the volcanological interpretation, and assess the general quality/impact of the study. However, the results might become a standard for the understanding/interpretation of volcanic processes at Volcano. For this reason, we highly recommend a revision from a volcanologist expert in the processes acting under the volcano.

In Summary, we answer the primary questions proposed to reviewers by this journal as follows:
- What are the noteworthy results? Any work using seismological data from massive arrays like this is remarkable and valuable. The selection process in a volcanic environment is extremely challenging and addressed very well by the study. The interpretation of the results is grounded on very extended literature and a relevant amount of volcanological data and experience. The retrieved connection between the volcanic systems of Lipari and Volcano, with its deep source under the second, represents an important result for our understanding of the two volcanic systems.
- Will the work be of significance to the field and related fields? How does it compare to the established literature? If the work is not original, please provide relevant references. The work is original and represents an important improvement relative to the current geophysical understanding of the volcano.
- Does the work support the conclusions and claims, or is additional evidence needed? Further evidence is required in order to support all the work’s claims.
- Are there any flaws in the data analysis, interpretation and conclusions? - Do these prohibit publication or require revision? None of the flaws in data analysis, interpretation and conclusions we found forbid publication, but they require revision.
- Is the methodology sound? Does the work meet the expected standards in your field?
The methodology of the current study requires further work and clarifications to meet the standard in our field.
- Is there enough detail provided in the methods for the work to be reproduced? The details provided are currently insufficient.

Critical Comments:
1) Technique
a) 2-D group-velocity maps:
While the processing and quality assessment of dispersion curves are excellent, the technical description of how they obtain 2-D group velocity maps lacks clarity and details:
1. The only paper mentioned is [54], but the reader cannot rely only on that. The authors should say more about the experimental assumptions they make. For example, do they take into account finite frequencies, or do they use ray theory to describe wave propagation? They mention a "Nonlinear inversion", but it is not clear what they are referring to. If they use ray theory, does it mean that they take ray bending into account? Assuming ray theory, what algorithm do they use for forward modelling? Do they solve the Eikonal with the Fast Marching/Sweeping Method, or do they use a Shortest Path Network? Despite the sharpness required by the journal, it is their job to clarify these points.
2. The authors talk about refinements of the parameterisation (i.e., discretisation?), but they do not say anything about the type of basis functions they use. Do they use pixels? Do they use splines or sines/cosines? What does this refinement of the parameterisation consist of? Is it done a priori based on the coverage? Showing a figure to clarify is necessary.
3. The 1. authors do not discuss the inversion method. We guess they use an iterative approach with linearisation at each step, like the Gauss-Newton or Levemberg–Marquardt method. If this is the case, do they use some regularisation (Norm vs roughness damping.)? If it is roughness damping, do they use the first or second derivative of the model? How did they select the damping?
4. More generally, while the paper [54], developed by Cabrera-Peréz, is a starting point, it remains a theoretical paper that starts from concepts applied to the nonlinear inversion of seismic refraction profiles. To understand its full reliability, the authors must accurately develop and describe the model and approximations within this study, especially in the Supplementary Materials. For example, the authors use a test for „scales“ without clearly defining what this scale is: as it is, it appears redundant with Fig S3. Only by reading previous literature can one guess that in the case of Fig S4, scale is (maybe!) node parametrisation. The reader is supposed to get all the information necessary here without having to guess the steps that have led to the results.
5. The scale is selected based on 0.02º x 0.02º anomalies (Fig. S4), but the entire workflow and all results are interpreted at a resolution of 0.01º x 0.01º. This is inappropriate, and assessing with 0.01º x 0.01º is central to understanding eventual trade-offs in the increasing parametrisation strategy used by the inversion.
6. We need to understand why a single checkerboard test is shown for the group velocities (Fig. S3). The authors use five periods between 0.5 s and 2.5 s: the period is not declared for Fig. S3, and no resolution assessment is made for the other periods. Does the previous selection criteria require the same source station pairs to be available at all periods? This could be the explanation, but it would reduce the number of available data without reason.

b) Vs model (MCMC inversion):
We also have critical comments about the final Vs inversion:
1. The authors use a Bayesian inversion, but they do not show the resulting uncertainty anywhere.
2. We do not understand what their favourite model is. Is it the ensemble mean or the median? How far apart are the mean and median? Typically (certainly in our experience), when the mean and median are quite far apart, it indicates that some Markov chains are stuck in some region of the parameter space associated with a relatively high (low) likelihood (misfit) that is not associated with a sensible earth model. For example, high velocities at shallow depths and low velocities at depths can produce low misfits in the inversion of surface-wave dispersion curves. Still, such a 1D model needs to make sense geophysically, even within complex volcanic structures.
3. Regarding the Bayesian sampling, we need to understand how many models the authors save (among the accepted ones) in the iterations after the burn-in. This information is important because keeping all the accepted models in a perturbative approach (where each proposed model is proposed by randomly perturbing the last accepted model) means having a final ensemble that is highly autocorrelated, which goes against the Bayesian paradigm, whereby the various models that compose the ensemble are independent of each other.
4. To mitigate this autocorrelation problem, most Bayesian sampling software saves one model for every N accepted models. BayHunter does it differently: it saves them all, and at the end of the inversion, it selects a random subset of the ensemble. This generally works fine; however, the authors only run ~17,300 iterations after burn-in, which means that the randomly selected subset could still be affected by autocorrelations. Given this, we suggest increasing the number of iterations after burn-in to at least 100k total iterations.

2) Interpretation
a) Assessment and Figures
The paper's figures are of high quality and very well crafted; however, they do not consider the results of the checkerboard testing accurately, and novel synthetic tests appear necessary when interpreting features. This adds to our concerns about testing different group velocity maps for various periods.
1. The checkerboard tests are shown for horizontal sections and different periods, but parts of the areas cannot be recovered adequately. These parts are still present in the S-wave velocity maps (Fig. 2) and are sometimes interpreted. Fig. 2 should report only areas where the velocity model can be reconstructed at a level allowing interpretation (thus at a minimum of 0.01º x 0.01º), Fig. S3F. The shading on unresolved areas should consider the results of testing scales for 0.01º x 0.01º checkerboard anomalies.
2. Fig. 4 will be indubitably the one the majority of readers will remember, sparking interpretations about the volcanoes from different disciplines. This figure must better acknowledge resolution issues. Volumes below 2.5 km are defined as those where resolution is maximum and then starts to decrease: we strongly disagree. If looking at Fig. S7, only periods of 2.5 s (primarily) and 2 s (partially) have any sensitivity at this depth. Resolutions on the volumes below this depth might not even be at a scale of 0.02º x 0.02º. The authors effectively have no way to assess if the contrast observed in Figure S5 at 2 s is real with the current materials. The contrast is strongly dampened at 2.5 s. It is necessary to shade any volume below this depth for all figures, certainly avoiding drawing any interpreted feature in Figure 4 below this depth.
3. Anomalies H1 and H4 are both in the northern part of the study area, where resolution testing is negative. The two H1 anomalies have quite an important role in the interpretation [Lines 121-139]. Still, at present, its recovery cannot be considered reliable, even less its description as a spherical anomaly and, consequently, its interpretation. A spike test of the corresponding dimension could better prove its reliability. The authors only note H4 as it corresponds to the high velocities of [42], so its lack of recovery is not as problematic, but the lack of resolution should be acknowledged in the text. A second spike test would better clarify the resolution.
4. While L1 can be recovered in the resolved depth span, we recommend a wider synthetic test of L1 at all periods considered. This would provide stronger evidence that L2, and especially the low-velocity pathway connecting to Lipary through Vulcanello, are no ghosts.

b) Interpreted features
Here, we discuss interpreted features, highlighting where we find inconsistencies.
1. Throughout the paper, the authors make no mention of high-velocity anomalies that might correspond to crater rims. Velocity tomography (Di Stefano et al., 2002; Vanorio et al., 2005; Battaglia et al., 2008), including ANT results (De Siena et al, 2018) show that high-velocity shallow anomalies (< 1.5 km) like those recovered around L1 are the buried trace of such rims at 1 km (Figs. 2 and 3): the correlation with the crater rims shown in Fig, 1 of H2 and H3 supports this interpretation. This interpretation would greatly simplify the discussion and fit with the conclusions and discussions better than what is currently proposed.
2. The break in the high-velocity continuity around L1 in the NNW can be due to the collapsed caldera collapse, as discussed by the authors. In this case, we need to understand the role of H1. Are the authors claiming these anomalies are a signature of supercritical fluids? Are they a remnant of past intrusions? Suppose the anomalies can be resolved separately (see previous point). In that case, do we see them as forming a caprock for low-velocity fluids feeding Baia di Levante (see, e.g., Vanorio & Kanitpanyacharoen, 2015), as suggested by the „Sealing cap“ in Fig. 4 (but never mentioned in the text? Lines 121-139 should better clarify the geochemistry of the fluids involved, making the interpretation of the S-wave velocity anomaly unclear. From our experience, such an interpretation is challenging without measurements of Vp/Vs (Vanorio et al., 2005; Vanorio & Kanitpanyacharoen, 2015).
3. Line 171: Throughout the paper, the authors are very loose in the description of what magma is for them. Here, they write “The top of the magma is hypothesized.. “ What magma? A body, a sill, a mush? More generally, this is a problem in the text that could come back to bite from petrologists experts of the magma system. The interpretation of a low-velocity anomaly using Vs values is considered weak. The strength of having the anomaly correctly explaining both deformation and VLP models is indubitable. However, the work can be attacked without a correct petrophysical explanation of what type of magma is interpreted. Using current literature and petrological observations, such as those done by Jaxybulatov et al. (2014), appears crucial to mitigate criticisms.

3) Additional comments
a) The authors could specify if they add noise to their synthetics.
b) It could be more elegant to avoid the use of code lines in equations: the authors could use a mathematic one instead of VarRed in Eq. 1.
c) Abstract: “entered in unrest” or “entered into unrest”
d) Abstract: “and help discriminateing” as it still refers to “can”.
e) Line 168: We strongly advise against this sentence, which reduces the study's impact. The fact that it agrees with previous studies is likely not the concept the authors want to express; it is that the model resolves apparent contradictions between different interpretations of seismic and deformation models.
f) Adding the additional references in this review is not necessary for publication: they are only mentioned to clarify our points.

Best Wishes,
Luca De Siena and Fabrizio Magrini

The manuscript attributes differences between earthquake tomography and NANT to the volcanic
conditions present during field campaigns. However, earthquake tomography and NANT differ in the types
of waves analyzed: earthquake tomography estimates Vp and Vs models, while NANT relies on Rayleigh
waves, each of which responds differently to thermodynamic conditions. Additionally, earthquake
tomography typically has a more localized resolution. In my experience, variations in tomography models
can arise from differences in method or inversion schemes rather than purely from the properties of the
medium. Besides, the noise sources during the unrest period can have an impact in the cross-correlations
and hence on the tomography. For these reasons, it may be premature to attribute discrepancies solely to
the state of the volcano without considering methodological factors.
R: We address and present the discrepancies between these two different geophysical methods in the
Discussion section. We further explain how these affect their resulting resolution power and discuss the
potential reasons explaining the differences observed among these two kinds of tomography.
